chapter_theme: Twenty verses mix the renouncer's code (the defects of the soul, the path and timetable of release, the high state and the seven hells, the teacher's fitness) with the householder's giving, naming in sixes those to be fed, the gifts to students and ascetics, and the marks of love.

61.reading: The verse names desire, hatred, anger, partiality, avarice and pride without worth, and says that those rid of defect declare, by the scripture, that these are defects of the soul.
61.nuance: The six are called ஊனம், a flaw of the உயிர், not wrongs against others; the list holds the passions that Jain teaching treats as stains of the soul (anger, pride, greed) beside desire and hatred. ஒர்வமே is a rare form, read here as ஓர்வம் 'leaning to one side', and மானம் is pride, not the honour the word often means in the Kural.

items.claim: desire is a defect of the soul
hatred is a defect of the soul
anger is a defect of the soul
partiality, if that is the word, is a defect of the soul
avarice is a defect of the soul
pride that brings no worth is a defect of the soul

62.reading: The verse says that those who keep both scripture and conduct do not go to dances, festivals, weddings, killing grounds, the roaring battlefront or other such places, and that if they go it brings them lapse and loss.
62.domain_note: those bound to a rule of conduct; barring weddings and festivals points to the renouncer
62.nuance: Pleasures and violence are barred together: a wedding sits beside the killing ground. முனையுள்ளம் is probably for முனையுள்ளும் 'within the battlefront', and வேறிடத்தும் 'other places too' leaves the sixth item open.

items.claim: those of conduct do not go to dance performances
nor to festivals
nor to weddings
nor to the killing ground
nor into the roaring battlefront
nor to other such places

63.reading: The verse says that those who gave food, clothing, a stylus, a book and, with care, the leaf for figures and letters to those who live by hearing, writing and reciting will in this very life live amply, writing as they wish.
63.nuance: The gift is the material of study, and the reward named seems to be learning itself within this life (இம்மையான்), not a later heaven. பேணொடும் is read as 'with care', not as a sixth thing, so five things are counted; வேட்டெழுத is doubtful.

items.claim: giving food to students brings ample life here
so does giving them clothing
so does giving them a stylus
so does giving them a book
so does giving the leaf for figures and letters

64.reading: The verse reports that those who did great penance said release comes if one regards the Exalted one as the lord, recites the Exalted one's book, holds oneself in, and fully performs the Exalted one's hard penance.
64.nuance: உயர்ந்தான் is repeated three times, tying regard, study and penance to one figure. The order (taking him as lord, his scripture, then penance) is close to the Jain sequence of right faith, knowledge and conduct; that is our reading, not the verse's word. ஒப்புடைத்தான் is obscure. The verse does not count; the four items are the steps it names.

items.claim: taking the Exalted one as lord is the first step to release
reciting his book is the next
holding oneself in is the next
fully performing his hard penance brings release

65.reading: The verse asks whether one who wishes to see Death's strength cut down and who, delighting in the scripture of the all-knowing one and looking at nothing else, performs a pure high penance that harms nothing will not, having understood, rise to the upper world.
65.nuance: The penance must be ஊறுபாடு இல்லா, causing no injury, so non-harm is a condition of the austerity, not a separate virtue. பாலனார் and பாராது are uncertain; the question form (ஏறுமோ) expects 'yes'. The verse does not count; the three items are the conditions it sets.

items.claim: delighting in the all-knowing one's scripture is a condition of rising
looking at nothing else is a condition
a high penance that harms nothing is a condition

66.reading: The verse says that when the faultless learned who have searched its meaning describe the greatness of the stainless high state, there is no light, no speech, no opposition, no weariness, no trouble and no sweet sleep there.
66.nuance: The highest state is described only by what it lacks, and the list denies the goods of life (light, speech, sleep) as well as its ills; even rest is not offered as its pleasure. மாறு can be change or opposition.

items.claim: there is no light in the high state
there is no speech there
there is no opposition or change there
there is no weariness there
there is no trouble there
there is not even sweet sleep there

67.reading: The verse names sharp arrows, hot sand, hanging gems, the wet, smoke, darkness and the darkness beyond it, and says the great, having examined the scripture, declared these in order to be the seven low states of ruin.
67.nuance: We read the seven as the Jain sevenfold hell, whose names run from gem and gravel through sand, mud and smoke to darkness and great darkness; the verse's words fit that scheme only roughly, and கூரம்பு and ஈர்மணி தூங்கல் are hard to place. The sixth item is copied with its sandhi (புகையிரு ளோ(டு), 'with darkness' after smoke). The verse counts seven (ஏழு), not six, and we follow it.

items.claim: the state of sharp arrows is the first of the low states
the state of hot sand is one
the state of hanging gems is one
the wet state is one
the state of smoke is one
the state of darkness is one
the deeper darkness is the seventh

68.reading: The verse says that the gentle set out six qualities in those who love: dying for the beloved, giving wealth, sweet speech, delight in being together, pain at their pain, and grief at separation.
68.nuance: Love is defined by six acts and feelings, ranging from the gift of life to the grief of parting. புணர்வுலத்தல் is read as புணர்வு உவத்தல் 'rejoicing in union'; as written it could mean wasting away in union.

items.claim: dying for the beloved marks one who loves
giving wealth marks one who loves
sweet speech marks one who loves
delight in being together marks one who loves
feeling pain at the other's pain marks one who loves
grieving at separation marks one who loves

69.reading: The verse reports that the exalted set out lifting, bending, straightening, standing, lying down and moving as the six distinct actions that attend a living being.
69.nuance: The verse makes no moral claim; it classifies the body's movements. Why an ethics work keeps this list is not said; it may serve the Jain care over every act that could harm a creature, but that is a guess.

items.claim: lifting is one of the six actions of a living being
bending is one
straightening is one
standing still is one
lying down is one
moving is one

70.reading: The verse says that one who, knowing and without doubt, gave alms, begged food, food and clothing to those of hard penance will rule earth and sky in due order, every day, sweetly and without lack.
70.nuance: ஐயம் is used twice in two senses, alms in line 1 and doubt in line 2, so the gift must be given without hesitation. The reward is rule over both worlds, set out in order (வரிசையால்). The verse names four gifts, taking ஐயம் and பிச்சை as two kinds of alms.

items.claim: giving alms to ascetics wins rule of earth and sky
giving them begged food does too
giving them food does too
giving them clothing does too

71.reading: The verse says that one who arranged food for wayfarers, for those who bore heavy loads, for those lying sick, for kin, for those of the sky and for those of the other side lives fittingly in his own house.
71.nuance: The householder's table is set for six, most of them with no claim of kinship. வானகத்தார் with கேடின்று உடல்சார்ந்த is unclear (the dead, or gods); மறுதலையார் may be enemies or those of another creed, and பொறைதாங்கினார் may be porters or the forbearing.

items.claim: feeding wayfarers is part of a fitting household life
feeding those who bore burdens is part of it
feeding those lying sick is part of it
feeding kin is part of it
feeding those of the sky is part of it
feeding those of the other side is part of it

72.reading: The verse says that from not understanding comes fault, from fault comes karma, the one without understanding makes the karma that brings birth, and through birth the great suffering follows on, so that it becomes a circle.
72.nuance: The chain closes on itself (மண்டிலம்): suffering in birth feeds the same ignorance. ஒத்தான் and தொண்டு are obscure, and the exact links of the chain are our reading; the six items are the links of the chain as the verse names them.

items.claim: not understanding is the start of the chain
fault comes from not understanding
karma comes from fault
the one without understanding makes karma that brings birth
great suffering follows through birth
the whole becomes a circle

73.reading: The verse says that household life and great penance are both desired as noble ways of acting, and, as far as the words allow, that household life is letting go without clinging while penance is a clinging that is undivided.
73.nuance: Both ways are called வினைவாழ்க்கை and neither is ranked above the other; each is defined by its relation to பற்று. The second half is obscure: பாத்தில் may be 'without share' or 'without division', and the reading of it is tentative. The verse counts two (இரண்டும்).

items.claim: household life is a noble way of acting, defined by letting go without clinging
great penance is a noble way of acting, defined by undivided holding

74.reading: The verse says that the beauty of the waist, of the shoulders, beauty beyond compare, the beauty of gait, of modesty and of the neck are not beauty, and that the beauty of numbers and letters alone is beauty.
74.nuance: The six rejected beauties are the conventional marks of a woman's body, and the list includes modesty, a virtue, among them. Learning is named as எண் and எழுத்து, numbers and letters.

items.claim: the beauty of the waist is not beauty
the beauty of the shoulders is not beauty
beauty beyond compare is not beauty
the beauty of gait is not beauty
the beauty of modesty is not beauty
the beauty of the neck is not beauty

75.reading: The verse says that the fitness of a teacher lies in knowing the books of the six schools, holding to understanding, removing what runs against the doctrine, and refuting the contrary words of a false teacher.
75.nuance: The teacher is defined as a debater: he must know the rival systems in order to answer them. மறுவரவு and மாசாரியன் are hard: the second is read as மாசு ஆரியன், a stained teacher, set against ஆசாரியன். The verse does not count; the four items are the parts of fitness it names.

items.claim: knowing the books of the six schools is part of a teacher's fitness
holding to understanding is part of it
removing what runs against the doctrine is part of it
refuting the contrary word of a false teacher is part of it

76.reading: The verse tells a woman with spear-like eyes that, examining what one can do of the good things possible, giving brings enjoyment, penance brings heaven, and the penance that does not cling brings release.
76.nuance: The three are a ladder of means and fruits, and the top rung is a further kind of penance, not knowledge. அடையாத் தவம் is read as penance that holds to nothing; it could be penance that does not stop. The verse names three means and fruits, not six things.

items.claim: those who give gain enjoyment
by penance one gains heaven
by penance that does not cling one gains release

77.reading: The verse says that one who wishes to end the suffering and harm of the four states of birth and, examining the scripture's path, strives in penance to reach the pure state will gain release quickly, in three, five or seven births.
77.nuance: Release is given a term in births, not promised at once. நாற்கதி is the four states of birth of Jain teaching; வல்லைளீ(டு) is read as வல்லை வீடு 'release quickly', which the sense requires. The items are the three spans of births the verse names, not a list of things.

items.claim: release may come in three births
or in five
or in seven

78.reading: The verse says that those who keep and give to the motherless child, the widow, those whose living has lost its means, those ruined in trade, those who lost the wealth that fed them and the blind will live well.
78.nuance: Each recipient is named by what was lost (mother, husband, livelihood, trade, wealth, sight), so the list is of the newly helpless. வைத்து வழங்கி asks that one keep in order to give. வாயிழந்த may also mean the mute.

items.claim: giving to the motherless child brings a good life
so does giving to the widow
so does giving to those whose living lost its means
so does giving to those ruined in trade
so does giving to those who lost the wealth that fed them
so does giving to the blind

79.reading: The verse says that death, ruin, enmity, sorrow, joy and banishment from the land all come by the tongue, and, as far as the obscure close allows, that one's character is what passes the lips when speech suits friends.
79.nuance: Joy stands among the outcomes, so the tongue is the source of good as well as ill. நாக்காடு and the last two lines are obscure; நாட்டறை போக்கு is read as exile from one's country.

items.claim: death comes by the tongue
ruin comes by it
enmity comes by it
sorrow comes by it
joy also comes by it
banishment from the land comes by it

80.reading: The verse says that those who gave food to and were a spring of help for outcastes, the wounded, the blind, those unable to move, those who have lost their former state and the eminent will live as kings, giving audience among their people.
80.nuance: புலையாளர் is a caste term for those of outcaste birth; here it heads a list of people to be fed, marking a low station rather than barring contact. போக்கில் நிலையாளர் is read as those who cannot move, and தலையாளர் as the eminent fallen on need; both are doubtful.

norm.note: a birth-rank term of the period names outcastes as a class among the needy; the verse sets no bar on them

items.claim: feeding outcastes brings the life of a king
so does feeding the wounded
so does feeding the blind
so does feeding those unable to move
so does feeding those who lost their former state
so does feeding the eminent in need

links.note: Kural 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, whose very names must perish; Elathi 61 names six defects of the soul.
links.teaches: Together they show the Jain list keeping desire and anger but trading the Kural's confusion for pride, avarice, hatred and partiality, so the root faults shift from error of mind to faults of self-regard.
links.list_adds: It doubles the Kural's three into six and adds pride and avarice, which 360 does not name, so the passions are counted as the Jain stains of the soul rather than as a triad of the mind.

links.note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at the killing ground, the gaming place and the like; Elathi 62 says those of conduct do not go to dances, festivals, weddings, killing grounds or the battlefront.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses show that the book's bar is on spectacle as such: 12 keeps the eye from scenes of violence, and 62 puts weddings and festivals under the same bar and names the cost of going.

links.note: Elathi 9 says those who give food, shelter and clothing to the destitute live as learned men; Elathi 63 says those who give food, clothing, stylus and book to students live amply in this life.
links.teaches: The pair shows the book twice making learning or its fruit the reward of a gift, and 63 narrowing the gift to the tools of study, so that the giver shares in the learning he supplies.

links.note: Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Elathi 64 orders taking the Exalted one as lord, reciting his book, restraint and penance into a path to release.
links.teaches: The couplet makes worship the condition of learning, and the verse turns that condition into the first step of a sequence that ends in release, so worship, study and penance become stages rather than separate duties.
links.list_adds: It sets worship first in a ranked series of four steps ending in release, where the couplet only binds learning to worship.

links.note: Kural 269 says that even leaping past death is possible for those who have the power of austerity; Elathi 65 says that one who would see Death's strength cut down must study the all-knowing one's book and do a penance that harms nothing.
links.teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse names the conditions the Kural leaves out: the austerity that defeats death must be guided by scripture and must injure no creature, so non-harm becomes part of the power over death.
links.list_adds: It turns the Kural's bare power of austerity into a sequence of conditions (scripture, undistracted mind, harmless penance), each needed for the same victory over Death.

links.note: Kural 369 says that when craving, the sorrow of sorrows, perishes, joy is unbroken; Elathi 66 describes the high state only by six absences, sweet sleep among them.
links.teaches: The Kural names the goal as unbroken joy, while Elathi refuses even sleep's sweetness to it, so the pair shows two ways of naming release: as fullness of joy or as the cessation of every state, pleasant or painful.
links.list_adds: It defines the goal by a list of negations that strikes out goods (light, speech, sleep) along with ills, which the couplet's single positive term does not do.

links.note: Elathi 66 describes the high state by six things it lacks; Elathi 67 names the seven low states one by one.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses map both ends of the same cosmos: the summit is known only by negation, while the depths are given names and an order, so the book makes ruin more nameable than release.

links.note: Kural 72 says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Elathi 68 names dying for the beloved first among six marks of love.
links.teaches: The couplet states love's self-surrender as a claim about ownership, and the verse spells out what that surrender does in practice, from giving life and wealth down to grieving at a parting.
links.list_adds: It ranks love's marks from the gift of life down to feeling at union and parting, so the bones of 72 head a list that also counts speech and grief as love.

links.note: Kural 263 asks whether the others have forgotten penance in wanting to provide for those who renounced; Elathi 70 says the one who gives alms, food and clothing to ascetics will rule earth and sky.
links.teaches: Where the couplet treats provisioning ascetics as the reason householders left penance aside, the verse makes that provisioning its own road to heaven, so the giver gains what the ascetic seeks.
links.list_adds: It lists the gifts in kind (alms, begged food, food, clothing) and adds a reward over two worlds, which the couplet's question leaves unstated.

links.note: Kural 43 names five to be tended (ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself); Elathi 71 names six to be fed: wayfarers, burden-bearers, the sick, kin, those of the sky and those of the other side.
links.teaches: Beside the Kural's five, the Elathi list drops the self and widens the circle to the stranger, the labourer, the sick and the adversary, so the household's duty is measured by need more than by bond or rite.
links.list_adds: It counts the sick, the porter and the adversary as equal claimants on the household's food, which the couplet's ancestral and kin-centred five do not include.

links.note: Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal for real; Elathi 72 traces not understanding to fault, karma, birth and suffering, and says it turns in a circle.
links.teaches: The couplet names ignorance as the cause of birth, and the verse adds the middle steps and closes the chain into a cycle, so birth becomes both the fruit and the renewer of ignorance.
links.list_adds: It sets ignorance at the head of six linked steps and closes them into a circle, where the couplet names only cause and result.

links.note: Kural 46 asks what a man who lives household life in virtue would gain by going the outside way; Elathi 73 calls household life and great penance two noble ways of acting.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks the household above renunciation, while the verse sets the two side by side as one kind of noble life defined by their relation to attachment, so the pair shows Elathi declining the Kural's ranking.
links.list_adds: It pairs the two ways under one name (வினைவாழ்க்கை) and defines each by how it handles attachment, where the couplet sets them against each other.

links.note: Naladiyar 131 says the beauty of hair, garment border and saffron is not beauty and that learning's beauty is; Elathi 74 says the beauty of waist, shoulders, gait, modesty and neck is not beauty, and that of numbers and letters is.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar dismisses adornment, while Elathi dismisses the body itself and even modesty, so the pair shows the same verdict for learning reached against two different rivals, what one wears and what one is.
links.list_adds: It replaces the Naladiyar's adornments with six parts and graces of the body, modesty among them, so the rejection reaches a virtue as well as looks.

links.note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Elathi 74 calls the beauty of numbers and letters the only beauty.
links.teaches: The verse takes the Kural's very pair, எண் and எழுத்து, and moves it from the sense of sight to the standard of beauty, so learning is both how one sees and how one is seen.
links.list_adds: It sets the pair of 392 against six bodily beauties, so learning wins a contest the couplet never stages.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 33 says only he who leads one to the higher state is a teacher; Elathi 75 says a teacher's fitness lies in knowing the six schools and refuting a false teacher's word.
links.teaches: One verse defines the teacher by where he leads, the other by what he can defend, so together they give the Jain teacher's two tests: the goal he serves and his mastery of rival doctrine.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 35 says giving brings enjoyment, penance heaven and knowledge release; Elathi 76 says giving brings enjoyment, penance heaven and penance that does not cling brings release.
links.teaches: The two Jain works share the first two rungs word for word but differ on the third, knowledge in one and a deeper penance in the other, so the pair shows a live question within the group about what finally frees.

links.note: Elathi 64 says release comes to one who takes the Exalted one as lord, studies his book and fully performs his penance; Elathi 77 says such penance brings release in three, five or seven births.
links.teaches: Read together, the verses give the path and its timetable: 64 says what leads to release, and 77 says release is not immediate but measured in births.

links.note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is true giving; Elathi 78 names six kinds of the destitute: the motherless child, the widow, those without livelihood, the ruined trader, those who lost their wealth, and the blind.
links.teaches: The couplet defines giving by the recipient's want, and the verse names who the wanting are and how they came to want, so the general rule gets its cases.
links.list_adds: It names each recipient by what was lost (mother, husband, trade, wealth, sight), so the Kural's வறியார் become a list of the newly helpless rather than the poor as a class.

links.note: Kural 642 says gain and ruin both come from speech, so lapses must be guarded; Elathi 79 says death, ruin, enmity, sorrow, joy and exile all come by the tongue.
links.teaches: The couplet's two outcomes are spread into six, from joy to death and exile, so the pair shows speech held responsible for the whole range of a life's fortunes, not only for profit and loss.
links.list_adds: It splits the Kural's gain and ruin into six named fates, adding death and banishment, so the stakes of speech rise to life and country.

links.note: Kural 226 says relieving the hunger of the destitute is where the wealthy should store their wealth; Elathi 80 says those who feed outcastes, the wounded, the blind, the immobile, the fallen and the eminent in need will live as kings.
links.teaches: The couplet calls feeding a store of wealth, and the verse names the stored return (living as kings) and widens the hungry to include the outcaste, so the gift crosses lines of birth the couplet does not mention.
links.list_adds: It names the hungry one by one and puts the outcaste first, so feeding is extended across rank as well as need.

elathi 62 line 2: முனையுள்ளம் is probably for முனையுள்ளும்.
elathi 67 line 2: இரு ளோ(டு) is split by a space inside இருள்.
elathi 68 line 1: புணர்வுலத்தல் may be for புணர்வு உவத்தல்.
elathi 77 line 4: வல்லைளீ(டு) is corrupt; the sense requires வல்லை வீடு.
